analysis.one_liner: Lets merchants band together to negotiate credit and debit card swipe fees with card networks under limited antitrust immunity.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 19-16, but the full House never voted before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let merchants — from big chains to small shops — jointly negotiate the fees they pay to accept Visa, MasterCard, and similar cards, instead of accepting take-it-or-leave-it rates. Normally such joint bargaining violates antitrust law; the bill grants an exemption and puts a Justice Department lawyer in the room. The version that cleared committee required any fee savings to be passed on to customers or employees, and let small banks and credit unions opt out. It cleared committee but never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants of every size, especially small retailers who pay some of the highest swipe fees, gain bargaining power they cannot have under current antitrust law. The bill requires that any fee reductions be passed on to customers or employees, so shoppers could see some of the savings in prices. Cardholders also gain from required public disclosure of how interchange fees are set and spent.

how_it_helps.text: Merchants and card networks could jointly negotiate access rates and terms — currently illegal price-fixing — with the negotiating sessions observed by the Justice Department's Antitrust Division.
Any negotiated rates and terms must be the same for all merchants regardless of their size or transaction volume, ending the practice of smaller merchants paying higher effective rates.

The ten largest issuers, acquirers, and network owners must disclose itemized costs of running the payment system, and any agreement reached — including the components of the interchange fee — must be filed with the Justice Department and made public.

When merchants' access fees are reduced, the bill requires them to pass the savings on to their customers or employees, aiming the benefit at ordinary people rather than keeping it in merchants' margins.

analysis.who_pays: Card payment networks and the large banks that issue their cards would bear the cost, since collectively negotiated fees would likely come out of the interchange revenue banks collect on every card transaction. Consumers who pay by card could also pay indirectly if issuers respond with higher annual fees or reduced rewards — a common outcome when interchange revenue is squeezed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Card networks and big card-issuing banks

drawbacks.text: The core mechanism is government-supervised collective price-setting: Congress would exempt what is otherwise an antitrust violation, and if merchants and networks could not agree, the bill (as originally introduced) had a panel of judges set the rates for three-year periods — a heavy-handed substitute for market pricing.
The pass-through mandate covers 'customers or employees' with no stated enforcement mechanism, so some of the savings could simply stay with larger merchants instead of reaching shoppers.

Issuers regulated by the National Credit Union Administration or with under $1 billion in assets can opt out of the negotiations, which could leave a separate fee structure for cards issued by smaller institutions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential savings are real — interchange fees are a percentage of nearly every card purchase and are baked into retail prices — and the bill is unusual in explicitly directing the savings to customers or employees. But the design is blunt: it trades antitrust enforcement for administered bargaining, the pass-through requirement is hard to enforce, and part of the savings could come back to consumers as higher card fees or thinner rewards. On balance it targets a genuine market power problem with an imperfect tool.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Judiciary Committee on a 19-16 vote and was placed on the House calendar on October 3, 2008, but the full House never took it up before the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers (D-MI) introduced the bill on March 6, 2008, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Rep. Chris Cannon (R-UT), and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee's Task Force on Competition Policy and Antitrust Laws held a hearing on May 15, 2008.
The full committee marked the bill up on July 16, 2008 and ordered it reported with amendments by a vote of 19 to 16 — a narrow margin that showed substantial opposition even inside the committee.

The committee-added amendments required disclosure of issuers' costs and interchange fee components, put a Justice Department representative in every negotiating session, created an opt-out for small banks and credit unions, and required fee savings to be passed on to customers or employees.
The committee reported the amended bill on October 3, 2008 (H. Rept. 110-913) and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 588, which means it was eligible for House floor action.
The House never voted on the bill, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Card networks and large card-issuing banks are better off: they kept the power to set interchange fees without facing collective merchant negotiation or public disclosure of how the fees are set. Merchants and shoppers got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Card networks and large card-issuing banks

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 27 Democrats and 18 Republicans cosponsored, and the committee vote to report it was 19-16 — but the bill never got the floor vote where partisan lines would have been tested.

industries.note: The bill strips these networks of the power to set take-it-or-leave-it access fees and forces public disclosure of how interchange fees are built and spent. Today merchants must accept the posted rate or lose access to nearly every card-accepting consumer.

Interchange fees are a major revenue stream on every card transaction; collectively negotiated fees would likely reduce it. Issuers under $1 billion in assets and credit unions can opt out, so the cost falls on the largest institutions.

industries.industry: Merchants and retailers, especially small businesses
industries.note: Small merchants often pay the highest effective card fees and have zero bargaining power against the networks. The bill gives them joint negotiating rights and requires any savings to flow to customers or employees.
